Headline: Timeline of Buddhism in Lanka
Text: Important events in the life of Buddhism on the island of Lanka, today known as Sri Lanka

Headline: Arrival of Prince Vijaya
Text: Prince Vijaya (Sinhala:විජය) (c. 543–505 BCE) was a legendary king of Tambapanni, based in modern day Sri Lanka. His reign was first mentioned in Mahāvaṃsa. He is said to have came to Sri Lanka with seven hundred followers after being banished from Sinhapura. —Wikipedia

Headline: Anuradhapura kingdom
Text: The Kingdom of Anuradhapura (Sinhala: අනුරාධපුර රාජධානිය, translit: Anurādhapura Rājadhāniya, named for its capital city, was the second established Sinhalese kingdom of ancient Sri Lanka. According to the Mahāvaṃsa, it was founded by King Pandukabhaya in 437 BC, whose authority extended throughout the country.

Headline: Reign of King Devanampiya Tissa
Text: Devanampiya Tissa (දේවානම්පිය තිස්ස, lit. 'Loved by Gods') was one of the earliest kings of Sri Lanka based at the ancient capital of Anuradhapura. His reign was notable for the arrival of Buddhism in Sri Lanka. The primary source for his reign is the Mahavamsa, which in turn is based on the more ancient Dipavamsa.

Headline: Arahant Mahinda arrives in Lanka
Text:
Arahant Mahinda (Sinhala: මිහිඳු මහරහතන් වහන්සේ/mihin̆du maharahatan vahanse) (285 BCE – 204 BCE) was an Indian Buddhist monk who brought Buddhism to Sri Lanka.He was a Mauryan prince and the first-born son of Emperor Ashoka, and the older brother of Princess Sanghamitra.

Mahinda was sent as a Buddhist missionary to the Anuradhapura Kingdom in Sri Lanka. Mahinda attained arhatship and resided at Mihintale.
Media Credit: Dennis Sylvester Hurd, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
Media Caption: Missaka Pawwa in Mihintale, where the Arahath Mahinda landed. This is also known as Aradhana Gala.

Headline: Initial construction of Ruwanweli Maha Seya
Text: Ruwanweli Maha Seya was built by Sinhalese King Dutugemunu in c. 140 B.C. It goes by many names including  Maha Thupa (lit. 'the Great Thupa'), Swarnamali Seya, Svaṇṇamāli Mahaceti (in Pali) and Rathnamali Seya. The stupa is one of the world's tallest ancient monuments, standing at 103 m (338 ft) and with a circumference of 290 m (951 ft). The original stupa had been about 55 m (180 ft) in height and was renovated by many kings.
Media Caption: Ruwanweli Maha Seya as it appears today. Located in Anuradhapura.

Headline: Polonnaruwa period
Text: The Kingdom of Polonnaruwa was the second major Sinhalese kingdom of Sri Lanka. It lasted from 1055 under Vijayabahu I to 1212 under the rule of Lilavati. The Kingdom of Polonnaruwa came into being after the Anuradhapura Kingdom was invaded by Chola forces under Rajaraja I and led to formation of the Kingdom of Ruhuna, where the Sinhalese Kings ruled during Chola occupation.
Media Caption: Stone statues in the Gal Vihara

Headline: Kingdom of Koṭṭe
Text: The Kingdom of Kotte (Sinhala: කෝට්ටේ රාජධානිය,), named after its capital, Kotte, was a Sinhalese kingdom that flourished in Sri Lanka during the 15th century. The Kotte Kingdom was largely dissolved during the Sinhalese-Portuguese War, as it faced attacks from rival Sinhalese kingdoms, the Kingdom of Sitawaka and Kingdom of Kandy.

Headline: Portuguese Occupation
Text:
Portuguese Ceylon (Portuguese: Ceilão Português, Sinhala: පෘතුගීසි ලංකාව Puruthugisi Lankawa, Tamil: போர்த்துக்கேய இலங்கை Porthukeya Ilankai) is the name given to the territory on Ceylon, modern-day Sri-Lanka, controlled by the Portuguese Empire between 1597 and 1658. (Wikipedia) Unlike the later Dutch and British occupation, the Portugues used overt violence to try to crush local religious practices by destroying places of worship.

Headline: Dutch Occupation
Text: Dutch Ceylon (Sinhala: ලන්දේසි ලංකාව Landesi Lankava) was a governorate established in present-day Sri Lanka by the Dutch East India Company. Although the Dutch managed to capture most of the coastal areas in Sri Lanka they were never able to control the Kandyan Kingdom located in the interior of the island. Dutch Ceylon existed from 1640 until 1796. (Wikipedia)

Headline: Life of Weliwita Sri Saranankara Thero
Text: Weliwita Sri Saranankara Thero (19 June 1698 – 18 July 1778) was the last Sangharaja of Sri Lanka. He was the pioneer in the revival of Buddhism in Sri Lanka, after the decline of the religion in the 17th and 18th centuries. Saranankara Thero was bestowed with the a title by king Kirthi Sri Rajasinghe in 1753, the same year he received the Upasampada (higher ordination of Buddhist monks) and re-established the Upasampada in Sri Lanka with the help of Mahasangha in Siam. He is also credited with the establishment of Silvath Samagama (pious group), a union of monks who lived in accordance with the Buddhist monastic discipline. (Wikipedia)

Headline: First Printing Press
Text: In 1734, the Dutch Government established the first printing press in Sri Lanka, primarily to serve the needs of both missionaries and administrators. The first Buddhist controlled printing press did not come to the island for another 128 years.

Headline: First Sinhala Moveable Type Produced
Text:
In 1737, an armorer named Gabriel Baas forged the first Sinhala moveable type. Because the presses were controlled by the occupying force, this technology would only be used for government and Christian religious publications for many decades.

Read more: The Revolutionary Sinhalese Press: How Print Technology Transformed a Nation

Headline: Weliwita Sri Saranankara Thero ordained and appointed Sangharaja
Text: Weliwita Sri Saranankara Thero recieved high ordination by the deligation from Thailand on the Esala poya day in 1753 at the Malwatu Maha Viharaya. He was soon after appointed Sangharaja by king King Kirti Sri Rajasinha. (Wikipedia)

Headline: British Occupation
Text: British Ceylon refers to the imperial possessions of the United Kingdom in the island of Ceylon, present-day Sri Lanka, between 1796 and 4 February 1948. Initially, the area it covered did not include the Kingdom of Kandy, which was a protectorate, but from 1817 to 1948 the British possessions included the whole island. The British Ceylon period is the history of Sri Lanka between 1815 and 1948.

Headline: Ven. Migettuwatte Gunananda Thera (පූජ්‍ය මිගෙට්ටුවත්තේ ගුණානන්ද හිමි)
Text: Ven. Migettuwatte Gunananda Thera, or Mohottiwatte Gunananda Thera, is known for leading the Buddhist side in debates between Buddhists and Christians in Baddegama, Udanwita, Waragoda, Liyanagemulla, Gampola, and Panadura, where the most famous of the debates took place. As a result of the debates, Buddhism in Sri Lanka saw a revival. (Wikipedia)

Headline: Hikkaduwe Sri Sumangala Thera (හික්කඩුවේ ශ්‍රි සුමංගල නාහිමි)
Text: Hikkaduwe Sri Sumangala Thera was one of the pioneers of the Sri Lankan Buddhist revivalist movement in the 19th century. He was the founder of Vidyodaya Pirivena, Maligakanda, in 1873, which was granted the university status later in 1959 by the Government of Sri Lanka. A veteran author and a fiery orator, he was a major figure in the Panadurawadaya, a religious debate held between Christian missionaries and Buddhist monks in 1873 at Panadura, Sri Lanka. (Wikipedia)

Headline: Founding of the Rāmañña Nikāya
Text: It was founded in 1864 when Ambagahawatte Saranankara,[2] returned to Sri Lanka after being ordained by the Neyyadhamma Munivara Sangharaja of Ratnapunna Vihara in Burma.

Headline: Founding of Jinalabdhi Vishodaka
Text:
In 1869, Ven. Dodanduwa Piyaratne Thera founded Jinalabdhi Vishodaka, the first non-monastic Buddhist school in Sri Lanka.

Ven. Piyaratne was a major figure in the Buddhist revival of the time. He also popularised the 'Poruwa' ceremony at Buddhist weddings.

Headline: Founding of Gangārāmaya Temple
Text: Founded by Ven. Hikkaduwe Sri Sumangala Nayaka Thera because of a lack of suitable large temple in the Colombo area. The land was bordered on two sides by the Moragoda Ela and the Pettigala Ela, on the bank of Beira Lake.

Headline: Publication of Buddha Ædahilla
Text: Ven. Gunananda publishes the first printed liturgical book, Buddha Ædahilla, that gave lay people the guidance for performing Buddha Puja on their own.

Headline: Founding of the Young Men's Buddhist Association
Text: The YMBA, or Young Men's Buddhist Association, was created in Sri Lanka in 1898. The main founder was C. S. Dissanayake as part of a bid to provide Buddhist institutions as an alternative to the Young Men's Christian Association. Started in Colombo, branches were formed throughout the country. Wikipedia

Headline: Ruwanweli Seya Restoration Society
Text: Ruwanweli Maha Seya was covered by wilderness as of the 19th century. After fund raising efforts by a bhikkhu, it was renovated in the early 20th century. The Ruwanweli Seya Restoration Society was set up in 1902. Most notably the philanthropist Hendrick Appuhamy donated Rs 20 million in 1912 (approximately 611 million USD adjusted for inflation in 2021) for restoration works.

Headline: Publication of Vandana books for school children
Text: Two liturgical books for school children—Buddhopastānaya (Attending to the Buddha), and Sri Saddharma Mañjarī (Blossoms of Sacred Dhamma)—are published in 1905. These books were used in schools to conduct Buddha vandana and teach about Buddhism.
Media Caption: Buddha Shrine at Gamini Vidyalaya (a primary school in the upcountry)

Headline: Education Ordinance of 1920
Text: The Education Ordinance of 1920 prohibited the teaching of religion in state schools. As state schools were the main resource for Buddhist students, this prompted protest from Buddhist leaders leading to an ammendment in 1927 permitting the teaching of religion to students who requested it.

Headline: Clause 9 of Chapter II
Text:
Clause 9 of Chapter II in the Constitution in Sri Lanka, established in 1978, states:

The Republic of Sri Lanka shall give to Buddhism the foremost place and accordingly it shall be the duty of the State to protect and foster the Buddha Sasana, while assuring to all religions the rights granted by Article 10 and 14

Headline: Building of Public Buddha Shrines
Text: In the 1950's residents begin to build public Buddha shrines in their villages and neighbourhoods not affiliated with any specific temple. Locals take responsibility for their up keep and perform Buddha Pujas on their own. Building public shrines in this way was completely unregulated until 2008 when the Ministry of Religious Affairs and Moral Upliftment issued its first rules for the construction of religious monuments.

Headline: Civil War
Text: A civil war was fought in Sri Lanka from 1983 to 2009. Beginning on 23 July 1983, it was an intermittent insurgency against the government by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE, also known as the Tamil Tigers) led by Velupillai Prabhakaran. The LTTE fought to create an independent Tamil state called Tamil Eelam in the north-east of the island in response to continuous discrimination and violent persecution against Sri Lankan Tamils by the predominantly Sinhalese government of Sri Lanka. —Wikipedia

Headline: Jathika Hela Urumaya (ජාතික හෙළ උරුමය) party formation
Text:
The Jathika Hela Urumaya (JHU), less commonly known by its English name the National Heritage Party, is a Sinhala Buddhist nationalist political party in Sri Lanka. The JHU was launched in February 2004 by the lay-based, Sinhalese nationalist political party Sihala Urumaya.

The Jathika Hela Urumaya contested its first parliamentary election in 2004. All of its candidates were Buddhist monks. At the election, the party won 5.97% of the popular vote (a total of 552,724 votes) and 9 out of 225 seats, making it the fourth largest party in parliament.

Headline: Bodu Bala Sena (බොදු බල සේනා) Founded
Text:
Bodu Bala Sena, (Sinhala: බොදු බල සේනා, lit. 'Buddhist Power Army') also abbreviated as BBS is a far-right ultranationalist Sinhalese Buddhist organization, and a break-away faction from the right-wing nationalist Jathika Hela Urumaya party. The BBS generally opposes pluralist and democratic ideologies, and criticizes moderate Buddhists for their alleged inaction against the rise of other religions in Sri Lanka.
